image_description: A close-up, high-angle shot of a sea lion resting on a rocky surface. The animal is lying on its side with its head tucked down, eyes closed. One large foreflipper is prominently visible in the foreground, draped over a rock. The fur appears short, coarse, and brownish-tan, transitioning to darker shades near the flipper and head. The background consists of out-of-focus grey rocks.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Head is broad with prominent sagittal crest in males.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The head is angled downwards and partially obscured by the resting posture; the sagittal crest (top of skull) is not visible from this angle.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: External ear pinnae (visible ear flaps) distinguish from true seals.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: A distinct, small external ear flap is clearly visible on the side of the head, confirming it is a sea lion/eared seal and not a true seal.
Dark, stiff whiskers are clearly visible protruding from the snout area.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Fur is short and coarse ranging from brown to dark grey, lighter on ventral surface.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible fur texture matches the description of short, coarse hair. The color is a consistent brownish-tan, typical for sea lions.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body exhibits streamlined fusiform form of substantial marine mammal proportions.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible portion of the body shows a smooth, tapered curve consistent with a fusiform shape.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Males develop thick neck mane and are significantly larger than females.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The neck area is obscured by the head's position and the angle; cannot confirm presence or absence of a mane.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Foreflippers are large, broad, and hairless on underside used for terrestrial locomotion.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible foreflipper is large and broad. While the 'hairless underside' isn't fully exposed, the visible skin texture on the flipper appears smoother/less furry than the body, consistent with anatomy.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Hind flippers can rotate forward for walking on land.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Hind flippers are completely occluded by the body and rocks.
Only one side of the animal is visible; symmetry cannot be verified against the hidden side.

The transition from the head to the body/shoulder area appears somewhat indistinct and 'mushy', lacking clear anatomical definition of the neck muscles under the fur.
